note: Real excerpts from public datasets. Every expected score below was produced by running the shipped pipeline on the exact file offered for download, so the page and the tool cannot drift apart.

samples.title: Resting, one electrode
samples.about: A person sitting still with a single forehead electrode, before any task started.
samples.look_for: A high score. This is roughly the best a one electrode headset can do.

source.name: EEG dataset of consumer- and research-grade systems

samples.title: Resting, four electrode headband
samples.about: The same idea on a Muse 2. Two electrodes behind the ears, two on the forehead.
samples.look_for: A high score, and a note that the electrode agreement check was skipped. Four electrodes are too far apart to cross-check.

source.name: EEG dataset of consumer- and research-grade systems

samples.title: Resting, research cap
samples.about: A research grade dry electrode cap at rest. Dry electrodes need no gel, which makes them fast to fit and noisier than wet ones.
samples.look_for: A good score, but usually not as clean as you might expect from research hardware.

source.name: EEG dataset of consumer- and research-grade systems

samples.title: Blinking on cue, headband
samples.about: The same person as the clean headband example, one minute later, blinking every three seconds on a beep.
samples.look_for: A blink every three seconds in the timeline, because that is when the beep went. The forehead electrodes sit right above the eyes.

source.name: EEG dataset of consumer- and research-grade systems

samples.title: Blinking on cue, one electrode
samples.about: Cued blinking recorded through a single forehead electrode, which is where a blink is largest.
samples.look_for: Blinks found from one channel with nothing to cross-check against. This is the hardest case for any artifact tool.

source.name: EEG dataset of consumer- and research-grade systems

samples.title: Clenching the jaw, headband
samples.about: Cued jaw clenching. Muscle activity from the jaw is fast and spread across frequencies.
samples.look_for: A large muscle penalty and a big drop in usable time. Compare it against the clean headband example from the same person.

source.name: EEG dataset of consumer- and research-grade systems

samples.title: Clenching the jaw, research cap
samples.about: The same jaw clenching task on twenty electrodes, so you can see which parts of the head it reaches.
samples.look_for: Muscle dominating the breakdown, and the per electrode detail showing it strongest near the temples.

source.name: EEG dataset of consumer- and research-grade systems

samples.title: Head movement with failing electrodes
samples.about: Cued head turns with the eyes closed. Movement pulls on the cap and some contacts start to fail.
samples.look_for: Several electrodes flagged as bad, and electrode pops in the timeline. This is the recording most worth acting on.

source.name: EEG dataset of consumer- and research-grade systems

samples.title: A clinical recording that was filtered
samples.about: A 32 channel clinical recording. It samples at 200 Hz, which looks fast enough to see muscle activity, but the signal was filtered away above about 38 Hz before it was saved.
samples.look_for: Muscle reported as not assessed rather than clean. A check that could not run is not a pass, and this is the case that taught me to say so.

samples.title: With real eye and heart electrodes
samples.device: Research cap, 20 EEG plus 4 reference, 250 Hz
samples.about: A face perception study recorded with electrodes placed specifically to pick up eye movement and heartbeat, alongside the EEG.
samples.look_for: Blinks found from the real eye electrodes instead of guessed from the forehead, and a heartbeat rate reported with high confidence.

source.name: OpenNeuro ds002718, from Wakeman and Henson (2015)
source.authors: Wakeman, D. G. and Henson, R. N.
